prompt_recommendations.rationale: Two consecutive addition errors signal a prerequisite gap (multi-digit addition) that was never addressed.
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Rule: After two failed attempts at the same arithmetic subskill, pause the main task and run 2-3 short remedial items on that subskill (e.g., 'Quick check: 14+7=?, 24+7=?, 140+70=?') before resuming.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Targets the actual bottleneck rather than recycling the unsolvable parent problem.

prompt_recommendations.title: Vary problem types to prevent template repetition
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Both practice items used the same 'sum given angles then subtract from 360' template, limiting transfer.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: Four angles around a point are 80°, 60°, 70°, and x°. Find x.
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Rule: Across the session, vary the problem structure: include (a) finding one missing angle, (b) finding two equal missing angles, (c) verifying whether given angles can surround a point, (d) word problems.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Prevents mindless procedure repetition and tests genuine understanding.

prompt_recommendations.title: Signal diagram dependence explicitly or remove diagram references
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Tutor references 'the diagram' at turns 3 and 9 but no image is rendered for the student, risking confusion.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: Looking at the diagram, you can see 8 equal angles around a central point
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Rule: Only reference a diagram if one has been explicitly emitted in the same turn. Otherwise describe the configuration in words.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Eliminates dangling references and reduces student confusion.

prompt_recommendations.title: Tighten praise calibration
prompt_recommendations.rationale: After the student answered '350' (still wrong), the next correct MCQ answer got 'Perfect!' — praise should be contingent and specific.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: Perfect! You've got the fundamental rule
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Rule: Use 'Perfect/Exactly' only after fully correct, unscaffolded answers. After scaffolded recovery, use 'Right — and notice that…' style acknowledgement.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Praise becomes informative, not inflationary.

prompt_recommendations.title: Minimum-effective-dose instruction
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Turns 1 and 9 include long expository preambles before the question.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: Think about standing in the center of a roundabout and looking in all directions
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Rule: Cap instructional preamble at 2 sentences before each student action. Move analogies into feedback after a first attempt.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Increases student doing-to-reading ratio.

flow_recommendations.title: Add a retry-cap with remediation routing
flow_recommendations.rationale: Engine continued the main thread despite two identical arithmetic errors; a retry cap should reroute to a prereq mini-drill.
flow_recommendations.expected_effect: Automatic pivot to addition remediation when the same subskill fails twice.

flow_recommendations.title: Gate progression on mastery, not turn count
flow_recommendations.rationale: Student moved from rule discovery to application despite an incorrect '350' answer that was only patched by reveal.
flow_recommendations.expected_effect: Ensures the rule is genuinely retrieved before application phase.

flow_recommendations.title: Ensure diagrams render or suppress diagram language
flow_recommendations.rationale: Flags indicate figure_ref_without_signal at turns 3 and 9.
flow_recommendations.evidence_quote: Looking at the diagram, you can see four angles around a point

experience_recommendations.title: Softer error-message tone with encouragement
experience_recommendations.rationale: An error-prone student is repeatedly told 'Not quite' / 'That's not quite right' which can demotivate.
experience_recommendations.evidence_quote: That's not quite right. Let's add those three angles step by step
experience_recommendations.expected_effect: Maintains student confidence during a struggle sequence.

experience_recommendations.title: Render arithmetic on a number line or place-value visual on second failure
experience_recommendations.rationale: A visual representation could unblock the 140+70 addition mistake more effectively than another verbal prompt.
experience_recommendations.evidence_quote: What do you get when you add 140° + 70°?
experience_recommendations.expected_effect: Inline media supports the struggling addition step.

overall_summary: The session has a sound cadence of instruction-then-practice and correctly introduces the 360° rule, but it is undermined by weak handling of repeated student errors: the tutor reveals correct values rather than diagnosing the underlying addition weakness, never pivots to prerequisite remediation, and uses a single problem template that limits transfer. The student's error-prone persona is mishandled most clearly at turns 13–15, where multi-digit addition is the real bottleneck but never addressed.

bea_evaluations.tutor_excerpt: Actually, let's check that: 140° + 70° = 210°, not 200°. So the three known angles sum to 210°. Now ... 210° + x = 360°. What is x when you subtract 210° from 360°?
bea_evaluations.rationale: Tutor pinpoints the exact addition error and gives a clear next action (subtract 210 from 360), but guidance is weak because it simply reveals the correct sum after a repeated error rather than remediating the addition subskill.

active_learning.evidence: Session is mostly MCQ practice with student responses (turns 17, 19, 26, 33, 46), so student does most of the talking, but tutor sometimes over-explains (turns 29, 47).

direct_instruction_active_practice.evidence: Most teaching segments are followed by an MCQ, but some tutor turns (e.g., 22→23) chain explanation then question; also tutor occasionally posted just a stub like turn 39 'Let's practice with a calculation:' with no action.

deliberate_practice.evidence: On the scale denominator error (turn 33→34), tutor gave focused corrective feedback then student succeeded; however on river-distance problem (turn 37), tutor abandoned it instead of giving a similar varied problem.

mastery_learning.evidence: Progression seems step-based rather than mastery-gated; tutor moved on after single correct MCQ answers (e.g., turn 51 → new topic) without retrieval checks.

cognitive_load.evidence: Generally one idea per turn with bolded key terms (turn 29 large-scale vs small-scale), but turn 29 packs definitions, analogy, and answer reveal at once.

layering.evidence: Scale concept built on prior detail concept (turn 36 links 1:5,000 back to school-campus detail), but few explicit links across map-type topics.

non_interference.evidence: Thematic vs topographic vs political maps appear close together (turns 45-49); tutor does explicitly contrast 'you're thinking about what a topographic map would show' (turn 47).

interleaving.evidence: Problems mostly follow the same MCQ-on-scale template; numeric calculation question (turn 37) was skipped, so variety collapsed back to definition-recognition MCQs.

testing_effect.evidence: Tutor asks retrieval MCQs first before explaining (turn 23, 30, 40), but hints arrive quickly after a single wrong answer (turn 27 reveals definition immediately).

targeted_remediation.evidence: After student role-confusion (student impersonating tutor in turns 24, 38, 53, 61), tutor never diagnosed the meta-problem nor routed to prereq practice; just posted next MCQ (turn 25, 39, 54, 62).

strongest_behaviors: Clear, focused corrective feedback on the scale-denominator misconception with concrete numbers (turn 34) that led to student success in turn 35.
Consistent use of bolded key terms and contrasting definitions (turns 29, 47) that help distinguish confusable map types.
weakest_behaviors: Tutor repeatedly failed to handle student turns that impersonated the tutor by posing their own questions (turns 24, 38, 53, 61); the tutor simply ignored or re-posted its own MCQ instead of correcting the role confusion.

Tutor abandoned the open-ended calculation problem in turn 37 after the student gave a confused answer (turn 41), instead of remediating the calculation skill — a clear missed deliberate-practice opportunity.

prompt_recommendations.title: Forbid abandoning open-response problems
prompt_recommendations.rationale: When student answered 'the river is 20 kilometres long' to a question they invented, tutor dropped the original calculation task (turn 37) and jumped to an unrelated MCQ.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: I notice you calculated an answer for a different problem than the one I just posed! ... Let me pose the question I intended:
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Rule: If you posed a calculation/open question and the student's answer is off-topic or wrong, re-anchor to YOUR original question and walk them through it with subgoals. Do NOT substitute a new question until the original is resolved or explicitly deferred.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Preserves deliberate practice on the calculation skill instead of skipping it.

prompt_recommendations.title: Detect and correct student role-impersonation
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Student repeatedly produced tutor-style turns ('Okay, fantastic! ... Here's a problem for you:') and the tutor either silently posted a stub (turn 39, 54, 62) or moved on, never naming the issue.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: Okay, fantastic! You're really getting the hang of map scales. Here's a problem for you: On a map with a scale of 1:25,000, a river measures 8 cm long...
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Rule: If the student message looks like a tutor turn (praises you, poses a new MCQ, or invents a problem), gently call this out: 'I'm the tutor here — let's stay with my question.' Then re-post YOUR pending question.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Stops the role-swap drift and keeps the lesson on track.

prompt_recommendations.title: Hold MCQ answer reveal until at least one more guided attempt
prompt_recommendations.rationale: On turn 29, tutor revealed the answer 'option B' after just one wrong guess, undermining retrieval practice.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: So a world map that shows the entire globe would be a **small-scale** map - option B.
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Rule: After a wrong MCQ answer, give ONE targeted hint and ask the student to choose again from the original options before revealing the correct letter.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Stronger testing effect and reduced answer-leakage.

prompt_recommendations.title: Avoid empty stub turns
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Turns 39, 54, and 62 consist of one-line stubs ('Let's practice with a calculation:', 'Let's check your understanding.', 'Let's try this one:') with no actual content — wasted turns.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: Let's practice with a calculation:
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Rule: Never emit a 'transition only' message. Every tutor turn must contain either a question, an explanation, or feedback. Combine the transition with the next question in a single turn.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Cleaner pacing, fewer wasted exchanges.

prompt_recommendations.title: Explicitly contrast confusable map types when introduced
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Student confused thematic with topographic (turn 46) and then with political (turn 48); discriminating features were only stated reactively.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: Not quite - you're thinking about what a **topographic** map would show.
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: When introducing any map type, include a one-line contrast table with the other map types already covered (topographic vs thematic vs political vs street) before asking the practice question.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Reduces back-to-back confusion and supports non-interference.

prompt_recommendations.title: Add a brief retrieval check before changing topic
prompt_recommendations.rationale: After scale mastery in turn 36, tutor immediately jumped to a calculation (turn 37) without a quick retrieval check that locked in the rule.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: Great understanding of how map scales work! Now let's put this knowledge into practice with a real calculation.
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Before switching subtopics, ask one ≤20-word retrieval prompt that requires recalling the rule just learned, then proceed.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Supports mastery-gated progression.

prompt_recommendations.title: Vary problem types to prevent template repetition
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Several consecutive MCQs are 'identify the correct scale/map type' — student can pattern-match without deep processing.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: Which of these map scales would show the most detail for a small area, like a school campus?
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Rule: Interleave question formats — definition MCQ, numeric conversion, scenario justification, open short-answer — and avoid more than two consecutive items of the same format.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Better interleaving, deeper learning.

flow_recommendations.title: Detect tutor-impersonation in student turns
flow_recommendations.rationale: Engine should classify student messages and route 'tutor-style' ones to a corrective handler instead of letting the model post a stub.
flow_recommendations.evidence_quote: Okay, that's excellent! You're doing great. Now, let's talk about some other important parts of a map...

flow_recommendations.title: Block stub-only tutor outputs
flow_recommendations.rationale: Turns 39, 54, 62 are content-free; an output validator could re-prompt the model to produce a full turn.

flow_recommendations.title: Retry policy on open calculations
flow_recommendations.rationale: When an open numeric problem is posed (turn 37) and student's response doesn't include working, the engine should force a hint-and-retry loop before allowing topic change.
flow_recommendations.evidence_quote: If a map scale is 1:50,000 and the straight-line distance between two villages is 8 cm on the map, calculate the actual distance...

experience_recommendations.title: More encouraging tone after multiple errors
experience_recommendations.rationale: Error-prone student got 'Not quite' three times in a row early on (turns 18, 20, 27) which may feel discouraging.
experience_recommendations.evidence_quote: Still not quite right. Think about what makes a navigation app useful for getting around Victoria specifically.

experience_recommendations.title: Inline a small visual or analogy for scale
experience_recommendations.rationale: Scale terminology confused the student; a quick visual analogy (e.g., zoom-in/zoom-out icon) could anchor it.
experience_recommendations.evidence_quote: The scale terminology can be confusing at first, but think of it this way...
experience_recommendations.expected_effect: Reduces cognitive load on a known-confusable concept.

overall_summary: The tutor delivers a structured MCQ-driven lesson on map types and scale with generally clear feedback and good use of bolded key terms. However, the session is repeatedly derailed by the student impersonating the tutor (inventing their own questions), which the tutor never addresses — instead emitting empty stub turns and skipping its own pending questions, including the only open numeric calculation. Progression is step-based rather than mastery-gated, with quick answer reveals after single errors and limited variety in problem formats. Strongest moments are the scale-denominator remediation (turns 34–36); weakest are the abandoned calculation (turn 37→42) and uncorrected role-swap behavior.
